newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER-FRENCH REVERSAL ON PERIMETER FENCES.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-FRENCH REVERSAL ON PERIMETER FENCES.

text.p: France's new government, unlike its predecessor, is against perimeter fencing at the 1998 World Cup but will not alter French advertising laws to accommodate a U.S. brewery, Sports Minister Marie-George Buffet said.
"Most of the matches will be able to be played without fences," Buffet said in an interview released on Thursday.
The new Stade de France, venue for the June 10 opening game and July 12 final, is equipped with a system of removable fences, she told the Paris evening newspaper Le Monde.
She said Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's government, elected this month, would analyse each venue individually.

"We're going to advance quickly on this problem. A decision will be taken early in July in conjunction with the Interior Ministry, the French World Cup organising committee CFO and the municipalities," Buffet said.
World soccer body FIFA was unhappy with the previous French administration's plans to retain perimeter fencing against its wishes, saying fans were not animals to be kept in cages.

Buffet said, however, the government was against altering France's Evin law on the advertising of alcohol at sports venues to accommodate one of the World Cup sponsors, the Anheuser-Busch brewery which produces Budweiser beer.
"My position is firm, there will be no questioning of the Evin law. There will be no exceptions," she said.
Anheuser-Busch signed a contract with FIFA worth about 100 million francs ($25 million) for the right to advertise in the 10 World Cup stadiums during next year's tournament.

The Evin Law prohibits the televised broadcasting in France of competitions held in stadiums where there are advertisements for alcoholic drinks, although the advertising panels themselves are not illegal.
If French fans are to be able to watch World Cup matches on television, advertisments of alcoholic drinks will have to be banned at the venues.
